entities.name: Tintern Abbey
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Tintern Abbey in Monmouthshire, Wales, founded in 1131 as the first Cistercian abbey in Wales and dissolved in 1536 under Henry VIII, is the most evocative and culturally significant medieval ruin in Britain due to its extraordinary state of preservation, its location in the Wye Valley, and its central role in British Romanticism through William Wordsworth's 1798 poem 'Lines written a few miles above Tintern Abbey' — one of the most famous poems in the English language. The abbey's ruins inspired multiple generations of painters, poets, and thinkers.

Tintern was founded by Walter de Clare as the first Cistercian abbey in Wales, growing through wool trade wealth to become one of the most prosperous monasteries in Britain. The present church, built 1269-1301, is the finest surviving example of Decorated Gothic architecture in Britain. The abbey's dissolution in 1536 left the structures intact but roofless — nature gradually reclaiming the Gothic arches and windows in a process that Romantic observers found sublime.

Wordsworth's 1798 visit — five years after his first visit, on returning with his sister Dorothy — produced the poem that defined British Romanticism's engagement with nature, memory, and time. The poem's famous lines about 'spots of time' and the sense that nature restores spiritual sustenance represented a new way of relating to landscape. J.M.W. Turner's multiple paintings of Tintern (1790s-1830s) and the tradition of the 'Wye Tour' — visiting the abbey's ruins by boat on the River Wye — made Tintern the birthplace of tourism as an aesthetic practice.
